idiom_name: static factory methods on the class or interface (List.of, Optional.of, BigInteger.probablePrime)
implementation_notes: The JDK makes this the standard creation idiom, so no separate factory class is needed: List.of/Set.of/Map.of (JDK 9+), Optional.of/ofNullable/empty, Boolean.valueOf, BigInteger.probablePrime and Collections.unmodifiableList are all static factories on the type or interface, with constructors private and the declared return type an interface whose implementation classes stay non-public (List.of picks a private implementation by size). Factories also allow caching for value-based classes and turn failure into a documented exception or an Optional; the classic public constructor remains the right default when none of these motivations holds, because constructors are what IDEs and Javadoc surface first.
pitfalls: Static factories do not stand out in Javadoc and IDEs do not suggest them, so the class documentation must state the intended way to obtain an instance.
A private constructor removes subclassing, and a caching factory makes instances shared: value-based classes explicitly forbid relying on identity (no == comparisons, no synchronizing on them).
Serialization and reflection bypass the factory: a factory-managed singleton needs readResolve (or an enum) or deserialization will create a second instance.
